name: Neoteny

card.summary: Neoteny is the retention of youthful features into adulthood; in looks talk it refers to large eyes, a smooth, soft-featured face and other juvenile traits that people tend to read as attractive and approachable.
card.note: The term comes from evolutionary biology; its use as a facial-attractiveness framework is a popular extension.

quick.overview:
Neoteny is a biological term for the slowing of development so that adults keep traits normally seen in the young. In looksmaxxing it is used as shorthand for youthful facial traits: large eyes, a small nose and chin, full lips, smooth skin and a rounded, soft face.

People use the idea to explain which faces read as youthful, friendly or attractive, and to decide what to emphasise. Research in evolutionary biology and social psychology has examined neotenous features, including how perceived threat changes preferences for them.
quick.how: In practice, people use the concept as a lens rather than a procedure: they look at eye size, skin smoothness, facial fullness and proportion in photos and mirrors, then choose skincare, hair, makeup, grooming or cosmetic changes that keep or emphasise a youthful look. Many communities set it against dimorphic features such as a heavy brow and angular jaw.
quick.risks: The concept itself carries no direct risk. Critics of older neoteny theories point out that the idea has been misused historically to justify racial and sexist claims, and the facial-attractiveness version is a simplification of a much broader biological idea. Procedures chosen to chase a youthful look carry their own risks.

lead: Neoteny is the slowing or delay of an organism's development so that adults retain features seen earlier only in juveniles. The term was coined by Julius Kollmann in 1885 after he observed that the axolotl matures while keeping its aquatic, larval traits.[4] In human evolution it is discussed as one reason adult humans have a large head, a flat face and relatively short arms compared with other primates.[4][2]

In looksmaxxing, neotenous (or neotenic) describes faces with youthful traits: large, wide-set eyes, a small nose, a short lower face, full lips and smooth skin. It is usually contrasted with a mature or dimorphic look, and users discuss it when judging which features make a face seem youthful, soft or approachable and when deciding what to emphasise with skincare, grooming, makeup or procedures.

Researchers have studied neotenous features in evolution and in social psychology. Reviews describe a general trend toward neoteny in the genus Homo's facial development,[3] and an experiment on the Environmental Security Hypothesis found that perceived threat changed how desirable people with neotenous (larger-eyed) features were as social partners.[5]

angle.text: Neoteny gives people a vocabulary for the youthful end of facial appearance. Users apply it by emphasising eye area, skin quality and facial softness, or by keeping those features as they age.

paras: Kollmann introduced neoteny in 1885 in connection with the axolotl.[4] It belongs to heterochrony, changes in the timing or rate of development. In progenesis, by contrast, sexual development is accelerated rather than somatic development slowed.[4]

Louis Bolk argued in 1926 that neoteny was the central process in human evolution. Stephen Jay Gould later noted that Bolk's account was tied to scientific racism and sexism, while agreeing with the core idea that humans reach sexual maturity while the body is still in an infantile developmental state.[4] J. B. S. Haldane described the prolongation of childhood and delay of maturity as a major human evolutionary trend.[4]

A review of hominin cranial development proposed that modifications in facial development reflect dietary adaptation and, in Homo, a general trend toward neoteny.[3] Other reviews discuss how neoteny may have shaped human morphology,[2] how slow brain development lets caregiving shape the maturing brain,[6] and how prolonged youth traits are compared between humans and naked mole rats.[7]

Delbert Thiessen argued that primates have been evolving toward a flatter face, and Doug Jones proposed that sexual selection favoured neotenous facial traits in women, with neotenous male faces as a by-product.[4]

Communities use neotenous as a descriptor for youthful facial structure and apply it when comparing faces, discussing why some people look younger than their age, and weighing youthful against dimorphic traits. The same vocabulary shows up in discussions of makeup, skincare, hair and cosmetic procedures that preserve or emphasise a youthful look.

In two experiments with 96 and 80 participants, researchers tested the Environmental Security Hypothesis: as environmental threat rose, desirability of people with neotenous features fell. Participants chose between faces with enlarged (neotenous) or mature features after threat was manipulated, and the authors also tested an attribution-based mediation account.[5] Beyond this, much of the neoteny literature is evolutionary and developmental rather than clinical, covering species tempo,[1] human brain development[6] and cranial evolution.[3]

timeline.event: Julius Kollmann coins neoteny from the axolotl.[4]
Louis Bolk proposes neoteny as the major process of humanization.[4]
Pettijohn and Tesser propose the Environmental Security Hypothesis linking threat to preference for neotenous features.[5]
